## [Old Faithful]{.fragment} {.divider data-number="DEMO"}

<!-- Notes before the first `##` become their own blank slide, so the opening
     narration lives on this divider rather than the title slide. -->
::: {.notes}
Today I want to talk about using React.js within your Shiny applications. But
before I do that, I want to talk about my favorite Shiny application. *Everyone
remembers their first… app*, and mine was Old Faithful.

I have been building Shiny apps since 2016 and been on the Shiny Team since
2018. The Old Faithful app is the kind of app that made me love Shiny: one
input, one plot, a complete interactive application in just a few lines of R.

And this app is still Old Faithful in another sense: dependable, familiar, and
exactly the UI we have all seen before.
:::

## Ownership {.code-slide}

::: {.incremental}
- R owns both the UI definition **and** the reactive computation.
:::

::: {.columns .spaced}
::: {.column .fragment width="50%"}
```{.r filename="UI"}
ui <- bslib::page_sidebar(
  sidebar = bslib::sidebar(
    sliderInput(
      inputId = "bin_count",
      label = "Number of bins:",
      min = 1, max = 50,
      value = 30
    )
  ),
  plotOutput(outputId = "distPlot")
)
```
:::
::: {.column .fragment width="50%"}
```{.r filename="Server"}
server <- function(input, output) {
  output$distPlot <- renderPlot({
    x <- faithful$waiting
    hist(x, breaks = input$bin_count)
  })
}
```
:::
:::


::: {.notes}
The R UI is wonderful… until it isn't

- For an app like this, `bslib` gets you from nothing to something to be *proud of*
:::

<!-- The hook for section 02, and the slide makes its own argument with no
     annotation: skylighting colours an R string as a string, so the CSS and the
     JS inside these `HTML("…")` bodies render as one flat colour while the R
     around them is highlighted. That *is* what your editor shows you. Don't
     "fix" the rendering - the flat block is the evidence, and the X only names
     which part of it the talk is about.
     This slide replaced a `renderUI` one: dynamic UI was the wrong defendant,
     since `renderUI` is a perfectly good Shiny tool. The thing that hurts is
     authoring a second language inside a quoted string, where no editor,
     linter, formatter or test can reach it. It also pre-pays for the "Wait…
     what?" meme two slides later - by the time "You want me to write
     JavaScript?!?" lands, the room has already put its hands up to writing
     it. -->
## JavaScript, in a string {.code-slide}

<!-- The question is up on arrival rather than on a click, so the show of hands
     happens while the panel is still blank and the code lands as the answer. -->
::: {.nonincremental}
- How many of you have written JavaScript or CSS as a string in R?
:::

::: {.fragment}
```{.r filename="app.R"}
ui <- bslib::page_sidebar(
  tags$head(tags$style(HTML("
    .stat-card { display: grid; gap: .5rem; cursor: pointer; }
  "))),
  tags$script(HTML("
    $(document).on('click', '.stat-card', function() {
      Shiny.setInputValue('card_clicked', this.dataset.id);
    });
  ")),
  uiOutput("cards")
)
```
:::

<!-- Aimed at the JS body alone, not at the whole panel: the R scaffolding is
     fine, and an X over all of it would read as "Shiny is wrong". Measured off
     the rendered slide; re-measure if the block's length or font size changes.
     Its partner `.circle-mark` is unused for now - the "this stays" gesture
     belongs on the `## Ownership` slide if it comes back. -->
::: {.x-mark .fragment}
```{=html}
<svg viewBox="0 0 1019 329" aria-hidden="true">
  <path pathLength="100" d="M 16 14 C 300 118, 690 208, 1003 315" />
  <path pathLength="100" d="M 1001 20 C 700 118, 320 214, 18 311" />
</svg>
```
:::

::: {.notes}
*Ask it. Wait for the hands.* Then thin them out, one question at a time — each
one should drop some hands and leave the rest more committed:

- "Keep them up if that string was more than **ten** lines." *(most stay up)*
- "Keep them up if it was more than a **hundred**." *(fewer — and those are the
  people this talk is for)*
- "Keep them up if you wrote it without **one squiggly underline** telling you
  you'd made a typo." *(they all stay up; nothing in R was ever going to
  underline it)*
- *(hands down)* "And how many of you have thought about just using a **real
  JavaScript framework** instead?" *(hands again — this is the turn; the room
  has already had the idea, and the rest of the talk is permission to act on
  it)*

`bslib` got us from nothing to something to be proud of. Then a request comes
in — a distinctive interface, richer interaction, a component from a modern
design system — and there is no `bslib` function for it. So you reach for this.

And look at what the slide is showing you. All of that is one colour, because
to R it is one thing: **text**.

- Your editor thinks this is a string.
- Your linter thinks this is a string.
- Your formatter, your tests, your diff — all of them think this is a string.

It's a program.

So: you are *already* writing JavaScript. You are just writing it in the one
place where nothing can help you. Hold onto that — we come back to it.

I do **not** want to replace Shiny. The reactive data model is your domain
expertise. Keep Shiny for **reactive computation**, and use a modern UI
ecosystem — **React.js** — for the interface. React is not adding JavaScript to
your app; it is taking the JavaScript you already wrote *out of the string*.
:::


## React.js {.divider data-number="02"}

<!-- The room's reaction to the sentence before it, so it sits here rather than
     after `shinyreact` is introduced: the objection lands the moment React is

## Wait… what? {.meme background-image="images/wait-what.jpg" background-size="contain" background-color="#141519"}

::: {.notes}
At this point you might be thinking… "You want me to write JavaScript?!?"

<!-- The payoff for the show of hands two slides ago, on "JavaScript, in a
     string" - whose notes promise "we come back to it". This is where. Don't
     retire one of those slides without the other. -->
And the honest answer is: **you already do.** Every hand that went up a minute
ago was a hand that has written JavaScript. The question was never *whether* —
it is whether you write it somewhere your tools can see it, or inside a quoted
string where nothing can.

That is the big question in the room, so let's take it now. Joe Cheng has
always said Shiny authors shouldn't need to write JavaScript — and I believe
that still holds true.

Agents today have far more examples of mainstream React patterns than custom
Shiny UI apps. I trust any frontier model to write React.js code better than I
can. That narrow IDs-and-JSON contract makes the client boundary practical to
review and maintain.

Your job is to describe your UI and review the result.
:::

## Components {.code-slide}

<div class="hexreact corner"><div class="hr-atom"></div></div>

::: {.incremental}
- A component is a function that returns HTML-like markup.
:::

<!-- One component, defined once and used twice - the smallest honest picture of
     "user interfaces out of individual pieces". The right-hand panel is not a
     screenshot: it is the deck's own `.stats` markup, the same class names the
     JSX writes, so what you read on the left is literally what draws on the
     right. 272 is `nrow(faithful)` and 30 is the app's default bin count.
     The labels are written out upper-case there because the JSX upper-cases
     them itself - the point being that a component computes its markup, it is
     not a template. Change one side and change the other. -->
::: {.columns}
::: {.column .fragment width="64%"}
```{.javascriptreact filename="Stat.jsx"}
function Stat({ label, value }) {
  const name = label.toUpperCase();
  return (
    <div className="stat">
      <span className="stat-label">{name}</span>
      <span className="stat-value">{value}</span>
    </div>
  );
}
<Stat label="Eruptions" value={272} />
<Stat label="Bins" value={30} />
```
:::
::: {.column .fragment width="36%"}
[Rendered]{.render-label}

::: {.render-out}
::: {.stats}
::: {.stat}
[ERUPTIONS]{.stat-label}
[272]{.stat-value}
:::
::: {.stat}
[BINS]{.stat-label}
[30]{.stat-value}
:::
:::
:::
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
A component is a function that returns HTML-like markup. Define `Stat` once, and you use
it as `<Stat>` — twice here, and it draws twice. That is the whole idea: you
name a piece of UI, and then you reuse it.
:::

<!-- The id is kept from the old "UI is assembled from data's state" wording, so
     the published deck's slide address survives the rename. -->

::: {.notes}
React is *REALLY* good at just taking JSON and mapping data to UI.

You describe what the UI looks like *for a given state* — and don't worry about
managing the transitions from one data state to another!

Old Faithful is the whole idea in one picture: the same 272 waiting times go in,
`bin_count` reduces them to a `bins` array, and that array *is* the chart. The
only thing that changed between these two is the number. Nobody added, removed,
or resized a bar.
:::

## Old Faithful {#react-code .code-slide}

<div class="hexreact corner"><div class="hr-atom"></div></div>

```{.javascriptreact filename="app.tsx" code-line-numbers="|2|3,6|3,5,6|3,4,5,6|11|11-12|13"}
function App() {
  const [binCount, setBinCount] = useState(30);
  const bins = useMemo(
    () => bin_data(waiting, binCount),
    [binCount]
  );

  return (
    <main className="layout">
      <label htmlFor="bin_count">Number of bins:</label>
      <input id="bin_count" type="range" value={binCount}
             onChange={(e) => setBinCount(Number(e.target.value))} />
      <Histogram bins={bins} />
    </main>
  );
}
```

::: {.notes}
`bin_count` is the only state in the app. `bins` is *derived* from it — React
recomputes it when, and only when, `bin_count` changes.

Then the whole UI is described once, for whatever `bin_count` happens to be. New
state, new description, and React works out the difference.

Hold on to those two lines. In a few minutes the only thing that changes is
*where they get their values from*.
:::

## Why Shiny **+** React? {auto-animate="true" auto-animate-unmatched="false"}

<!-- The two marks as a corner lockup. They are the same `[data-id]` elements on
     the next two slides, so auto-animate carries them into the build and then
     into the finished logo. `.lb-shiny` is Shiny's own hex sticker, laid over
     the shinyreact logo; `.lb-hole` covers that logo's React atom, so what is
     underneath is the *Shiny* mark either way. See CLAUDE.md. -->
<div class="hexlogo lockup" data-id="hexlogo"><div class="lb-hole"></div><div class="lb-shiny"></div></div>
<div class="hexplus">+</div>
<div class="hexreact lockup" data-id="hexreact"><div class="hr-atom"></div></div>

- 🚫 Hand-rolled HTML and JavaScript in Shiny
- 🧰 Use the proper tool for the job
- 🤖 AI excels at building well-known frameworks

::: {.notes}
<!-- Do NOT ask for hands here: the "JavaScript, in a string" slide already did,
     and asking twice reads as having forgotten. Refer back instead - the hands
     are the evidence this bullet rests on, and they are already in the room's
     memory. -->
Those hands you put up earlier — that is this first bullet. It works, right up
until the app gets big, and then *you* are the framework.

I'm happy to do car maintenance with a multitool. But using the proper tool for
the job saves time, effort, and the skin on your knuckles. React is that tool:
it is what the rest of the world reaches for when a UI outgrows being
hand-assembled.

And it is the tool your assistant already knows. An LLM has seen millions of
React components and approximately none of your bespoke `tags$div()` scaffolding
— so building on a well-known framework is the difference between an assistant
that helps and one that guesses.
:::

## `shinyreact` {.tagline auto-animate="true" auto-animate-unmatched="false"}

<div class="hexlogo corner" data-id="hexlogo"></div>

<!-- The package's own tagline, in the quote treatment React's two get on "What
     is React?": a `>` inside a bullet, so the bullet's cyan rule and the
     blockquote's own border read as one double line. `.nonincremental` keeps it
     off the click sequence - it is the slide's subtitle, not its first point -
     and its own list, so the three bullets below stay a list of three. -->
::: {.nonincremental}
- > Shiny UI infrastructure for React-based component rendering
:::

- The Shiny server contains **only reactive data computation**
- The UI is a React client **you own**
- `shinyreact` ships **zero UI components**

::: {.notes}
With `shinyreact`, the Shiny server contains only reactive data computation, and
the UI is a React client you own. `shinyreact` provides the bridge between the
two and ships zero UI components itself.

Two frameworks, one reactive model: pure functional programming makes logic easy
to reason about as apps scale up in complexity, and that is what makes *both* of
these frameworks a joy to work in.

You build the whole UI from the ground up in React / TypeScript. It is an
experimental package, for the brave few.
:::

## Old Faithful, remixed {.divider data-number="04"}

## The server we started with {.code-slide auto-animate="true"}

<!-- The trailing `|` is an extra step that clears the highlight, so the
     auto-animate into the next slide only has to move the changed lines. -->
```{.r filename="app.R" code-line-numbers="|5|6|"}
x <- faithful$waiting

server <- function(input, output) {
  output$distPlot <- renderPlot({
    breaks <- seq(min(x), max(x), length.out = input$bin_count + 1)
    hist(x, breaks = breaks)
  })
}
```

::: {.chain}
[`input$bin_count` → `breaks`]{.chain-1} [→ `hist()`]{.chain-2} [→ `renderPlot()`]{.chain-3}
:::

::: {.notes}
Let's re-imagine our Old Faithful app using `shinyreact`.

We can see the single input value `bin_count` being used to calculate `breaks`.
That value is then fed into `hist()` with the specified breaks to produce a
histogram of the data.
:::

## The same server, with `shinyreact` {.code-slide auto-animate="true"}

<!-- Opens on line 5 rather than unhighlighted: the chain arrives reading
     `input$bin_count → breaks`, so the line that computes it is lit to match. -->
```{.r filename="app.R" code-line-numbers="5|6|7|4,8|"}
x <- faithful$waiting

server <- function(input, output) {
  output$distPlot <- shinyreact::reactive_output({
    breaks <- seq(min(x), max(x), length.out = input$bin_count + 1)
    bins <- hist(x, breaks = breaks, plot = FALSE)
    bins[c("breaks", "counts")]
  })
}
```

<!-- The chain carries over from the previous slide, so its first two links are
     unwrapped (no `.chain-N` span = visible on arrival). `bins` lands on step 1
     (line 6) and `reactive_output()` on step 3 (lines 4, 8); step 2 adds no
     link. See CLAUDE.md on counting the steps. -->
::: {.chain}
`input$bin_count` → `breaks` [→ `bins`]{.chain-1} [→ `reactive_output()`]{.chain-3}
:::

<!-- .after-code, not .fragment: this appears on the same click as the code
     block's trailing `|` step, which clears the highlight. See the theme. -->
::: {.after-code}
The computation is unchanged — **the value sent changed.**
:::

::: {.notes}
The reactive computation is unchanged. What has changed is the value sent by the
server.
:::

## `reactive_output()` — a [new]{.underline} concept

- No corresponding UI component on the server side
- Convert your data and send it to the client **as JSON**
- Send **only what is needed**
- Let React display your data's state in the UI

::: {.notes}
`hist(x, plot = FALSE)` creates a list containing `breaks` and `counts`. Now we
just send the required data — that is the contracted shape the browser receives.
Let React display your data's state within the UI.

There is no directly corresponding UI component. This is a new concept!
Where `renderPlot()` returns a regulated payload — HTML, or an image the
`plotOutput()` on the other end knows how to place — `reactive_output()`
returns nonregulated, raw **data**.

With this model, we are strongly encouraging the server to pass data directly to
the front end. The server sends facts; React does presentation.
:::

## The UI moves to TypeScript {.code-slide}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{.r filename="app.R (classic)"}
ui <- bslib::page_sidebar(
  sidebar = bslib::sidebar(
    sliderInput(inputId = "bin_count", ...)
  ),
  plotOutput(outputId = "distPlot")
)
```
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{.r filename="app.R (shinyreact)"}
ui <- shinyreact::page_react_html()
```

::: {.fragment}
UI inputs and outputs now live in TypeScript.
:::
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
Now let's look at the UI definitions.

Note that you're signing up for all UI inputs and outputs living in TypeScript!

<!-- Half of that "cost" is a refund, given the section-01 string slide. Say so
     here or the slide reads as pure downside. -->
Which sounds like a cost — and some of it is. But remember where we started: if
you were already writing the interesting parts of the UI as JavaScript in a
string, this is not new work. It is the same work, in a file, with types.
:::

## React {#react-ui .code-slide auto-animate="true"}

<!-- The React-only component from section 02, verbatim, so this and the next
     slide auto-animate as a pair: the whole JSX body holds still while the two
     declarations at the top rewrite themselves into the `shinyreact` hooks.
     Same construction as "The server we started with" above, and deliberately
     so - the server half of the app gets a before/after, and this is the UI
     half's. Neither slide may wrap its block in a `.fragment`: an element
     hidden on arrival has nothing for auto-animate to animate *from*.
     `useMemo` is written on one line, not the four the app spells it over, so
     the comparison is line for line: two declarations against two.
     No highlight steps here - this slide is the recap, and it is the next one
     that has something to point at. `code-line-numbers="true"` rather than no
     attribute at all, so the block keeps its line-number gutter: losing the
     gutter on one half of the pair would slide the whole block sideways. -->
```{.javascriptreact filename="app.tsx" code-line-numbers="true"}
function App() {
  const [binCount, setBinCount] = useState(30);
  const bins = useMemo(() => bin_data(waiting, binCount), [binCount]);

  return (
    <main className="layout">
      <label htmlFor="bin_count">Number of bins:</label>
      <input id="bin_count" type="range" value={binCount}
             onChange={(e) => setBinCount(Number(e.target.value))} />
      <Histogram bins={bins} />
    </main>
  );
}
```

::: {.notes}
You have seen this one already — the React-only Old Faithful from section 02.
One piece of state, one value derived from it, and the markup underneath.

Watch those two declarations at the top. Nothing else in this file is going to
move.
:::

## `shinyreact` {#shinyreact-ui .code-slide auto-animate="true"}

<!-- Opens lit on line 2 rather than unhighlighted, the way the server's
     after-slide opens on line 5: the pair has just rewritten that line, so the
     highlight is already where the eye is. -->
```{.javascriptreact filename="www/ui.tsx" code-line-numbers="2|3|8-9|10"}
export default function App() {
  const [binCount, setBinCount] = useShinyInput<number>("bin_count", 30);
  const bins = useShinyOutputValue<HistData | null>("distPlot", null);

  return (
    <main className="layout">
      <label htmlFor="bin_count">Number of bins:</label>
      <input id="bin_count" type="range" value={binCount}
             onChange={(e) => setBinCount(Number(e.target.value))} />
      <Histogram bins={bins} />
    </main>
  );
}
```

::: {.notes}
Same component. The markup did not move — only the two lines that say where the
values come from.

`ui.tsx` is built upon Shiny's `index.html` escape hatch, but upgraded for
React.
:::

## Two hooks are the whole API {.code-slide}

::: {.fragment .spaced}
```{.javascriptreact filename="read and write an input"}
const [binCount, setBinCount] = useShinyInput<number>("bin_count", 30);
```
:::

::: {.fragment}
Just like `useState` — except the state comes from R / python.
:::

::: {.fragment .spaced}
```{.javascriptreact filename="read an output"}
const bins = useShinyOutputValue<HistData>("distPlot", null);
```
:::

::: {.fragment}
R computes the value; React decides how it looks.
:::

::: {.notes}
<!-- The visual payoff for "JavaScript, in a string": that slide's
     `Shiny.setInputValue(...)` and this slide's `useShinyInput<number>(...)` do
     the same job, and the audience has seen both. One was flat green. -->
Compare the first line to what we had in section 01. Getting a value out of the
browser and into R was `Shiny.setInputValue('card_clicked', …)` — inside a
string, flat green, unchecked by anything.

Here it is the same job, with a **type** on it. Your editor knows `bin_count` is
a number. It will autocomplete it, and it will tell you when you get it wrong.

That is the whole trade: the JavaScript you were already writing, moved
somewhere it can be read.
:::

## The data cycle {.cycle-slide .nostretch}

```{mermaid}
%%{init: {"theme":"base","fontFamily":"Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif",
  "sequence":{"actorMargin":100,"width":300,"boxMargin":10,"height":50,
  "messageMargin":30,"mirrorActors":false},
  "themeVariables":{
  "actorBkg":"#141519","actorBorder":"#6FD4E8","actorTextColor":"#F2F4F8",
  "actorLineColor":"#A3ACBB","signalColor":"#00D8FF","signalTextColor":"#F2F4F8",
  "noteBkgColor":"#141519","noteBorderColor":"#A3ACBB","noteTextColor":"#F2F4F8",
  "labelBoxBkgColor":"#141519","labelTextColor":"#F2F4F8",
  "activationBkgColor":"#23252C","activationBorderColor":"#6FD4E8"}}}%%
sequenceDiagram
  participant B as browser · React
  participant S as server · R / Python
  B->>B: useShinyInput()
  B->>S: IDs + JSON
  S->>S: input$value → reactive() → reactive_output()
  S-->>B: IDs + JSON
  B->>B: useShinyOutputValue()
```

::: {.notes}
Top to bottom: a value leaves the browser through `useShinyInput()`, arrives as
`input$value`, moves through `reactive()` to `reactive_output()`, and comes back
to the browser as data through `useShinyOutputValue()`.

In Shiny for R or Python, that middle box is the app you already write:
`input$value` → `reactive()` → `renderFn()`. The only change is the last hop —
`reactive_output()` in place of `renderFn()`.

Keep R / Python for data work and reactivity. Inputs still travel to the Shiny
server; outputs now travel back as data.

IDs and JSON are the contract.
:::

## Testing {.divider data-number="05"}

## Test coverage at every hop

- **Within the server** — `testServer()` · `test_server()` · `local_server`
- **Server → client** — `wire_tap`
- **Within the client** — JS unit tests
- **Confirm the client** — `features.md`

::: {.notes}
The first hop is in-memory: the app's server function runs, the reactive graph
flushes, and you read the values back. No browser, no port, no waiting.

R has had `shiny::testServer()` for years. Shiny for Python shipped its own
`shiny.testserver.test_server()` in **1.8.0, released 2026-09-12** — three days
before this talk — plus a `local_server`
pytest fixture: name it as a test argument and you get a started session for the
`app.py` next to the test file.

```python
def test_doubling_app(local_server):
    local_server.set_inputs(name="Ada", n=10)
    assert local_server.get_output("greeting") == "Hello, Ada!"
```

`set_inputs()` returns once the graph has settled, so the next line reads the
result — no polling, no retry loop. That matters here because the React client
is gone in this test: what you are asserting on is exactly the IDs-and-JSON
contract the last section drew. The server half of a `shinyreact` app is
testable without any of the client half existing.

The other three hops, in a line each: `wire_tap` asserts on the `shinyreact`
messages crossing the websocket; the client's own unit tests are the agent's
choice of JS runner; and `features.md` is a nested list of features you can read
and other agents can confirm against.

<!-- Callback to "JavaScript, in a string": the third hop is only available
     because the client is a file now. -->
That third hop is worth a beat. The JavaScript in section 01 had no tests, and
could not have had any — you cannot unit-test a string. Getting it into a file
is what put it on this list at all.
:::

::: {.notes}
Five packages came out from under those apps, and each one answers a single
question.

`biobouncer` — is this even an identifier? Fifty sources, offline first, and
one shared conformance corpus across R, Python and JavaScript, so the three
cannot disagree. It is on CRAN, PyPI and npm. `bioclients` —
what do the sources say about it? Twenty-nine biological web services, one
table shape. `biohttp` is what those clients ride on: every call returns a
value rather than raising, with retry, a circuit breaker, and a cache that
stores only the successes. `biocohort` — which subjects and samples *are* this
study? The manifest, the subject table and every analysis output in one
validated object, with species and assay as values in the data rather than
types, so the same object serves any organism and any assay.

And `plotomics` — GPU-accelerated visualizations from one TypeScript core,
wrapped three ways: npm for React, htmlwidgets for R, anywidget for Python.
Headless factories, not React components, which is what lets one core serve
all three. Seventeen chart *types* in the package; twenty-six of them on
screen in the app you are about to see. Hold onto that one: it is what draws
the app two slides from now.
:::

## Plotomics Live {.gif-slide .nostretch}

<!-- The plotomics hex, parked in the corner the heading leaves free: this is
     the app the package from two slides ago draws. Markup rather than a
     `url()` in the scss, because quarto does not trace url()s out of an scss
     file and `images/` is not a project resource. -->
![](images/pkg-plotomics.svg){.corner-hex}

[**1,000,000** transcripts on the GPU · 26 visualizations · 65+ `reactive_output()`]{.gif-caption}

<!-- A recording of the deployment, not an iframe: it is a Connect Cloud app,
     and a served render makes no off-origin request. An `<video>` rather than
     a GIF - a million-point field is nearly incompressible as GIF (11 MB at 48
     colours and 6fps, and posterized), where h264 holds full colour at 25fps
     in 4 MB. Local file, so it is still offline-safe. See CLAUDE.md. -->
```{=html}
<video class="app-gif" src="images/plotomics-live.mp4"
       autoplay loop muted playsinline></video>
```

::: {.notes}
Xenium single-molecule transcripts. Every point is one mRNA molecule at the
micrometre where it was detected in a breast cancer section — not a cell, not
an embedding. The run found 42.6 million of them across a 313-gene panel, and
a million of those are drawn here, on the GPU, from React.

Watch the loop. They arrive — a million points streamed as binary blobs and
painted in one go. Hover one and you get the molecule under the cursor. Then
zoom, and back out to the whole section: the red is tumour epithelium, the
teal is stroma, and none of that structure is drawn by anything in R. R sent
the numbers.

The ggplot2 toggle is right there in the same panel, and on this page it has
to fall back to a subsample. That contrast is the argument.

Twenty-six visualizations, and the server publishes sixty-nine
`reactive_output()` feeds to serve them: twenty-two data feeds React reads
through `useShinyOutputValue`, twenty-eight ggplot2 PNGs for the classic side,
and the rest stats and config.

Two things to say out loud about that:

- `app.R` is **compute-only** — one `reactive_output()` per visualization, and
  not one line of it is UI
- the entire UI, in R, is **one line**: `page_react_html("www/index.html")`

If there is time, the Xenium page is not even the biggest thing here. Another
page draws a UMAP of 584,000 cells, and it ships as about **seven megabytes of
binary typed arrays** — R to the browser to the GPU, rather than
server-rendering the view. And because React owns the component, a new
selection updates the data in place: the visualization is never re-mounted, so
the GPU buffers are not reallocated on every click. That is the part you cannot
get from an htmlwidget without writing the lifecycle yourself.

Samuel puts it better than I do: R stays the analysis engine, React becomes the
visualization layer, and `shinyreact` removes what used to sit between them —
the custom JS bindings, the manual message passing, the serialization.
:::

## What's next {.divider data-number="07"}

## Future work: incremental adoption

- Embed React components into **existing** apps
- Wrap `shinyreact` in your own package!

::: {.notes}
Incremental adoption makes it so you don't have to port your whole application
into React.js.

It also opens the door for helper packages down the road: wrap a component you
have built in `shinyreact` and ship it as a package, the way `bslib` and
friends ship theirs.

Today, everything will feel ad-hoc when writing `shinyreact` apps — that is the
tradeoff of an experimental package.
:::

## Q & A {.divider data-number="08" visibility="hidden"}

## Is node.js needed? {visibility="hidden"}

- **No** — but highly recommended
- TSX is much more readable than vanilla JavaScript
- A build system can lint and strongly type your code

::: {.notes}
<!-- The third bullet is the direct answer to the section-01 string slide - lean
     on it if this question comes up. -->
That last bullet is the whole reason we started where we did. The complaint
about JavaScript in a string was never about JavaScript — it was that nothing
could lint it, type it, or format it. A build step is what buys all three back.
:::

## How do I review generated code? {visibility="hidden"}

- Unit tests help with drift — but they confirm *existing* behavior
- The logic you care about lives server-side: review it, defend it, write independent tests
- I'm comfortable delegating busy-work UI details to the LLM

## What about my existing apps? {visibility="hidden"}

- Agent Skills are available to convert Shiny apps to `shinyreact`

## Can I keep my existing outputs? {visibility="hidden"}

- **Yup.** Use regular render methods, just like normal
- Pair them with `<ShinyOutput id="distPlot" />` in your React code
- Don't reinvent the wheel — your UI app becomes more about **layout** than outputs
